entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: pree-dih-FYND. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: decided or established before an activity begins

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Adjective indicating that something was established beforehand; here, the labels would have been specified before learning.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: defining something in advance can be useful or restrictive depending on the task.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Explanatory here: the sentence identifies what is absent in this way of finding patterns.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in technical and professional writing. “Defined in advance” is a clearer everyday paraphrase.

when_to_use: Describe rules, options, labels or limits specified before they are used.
when_not_to_use: Do not use predefined simply to mean correct or suitable; it tells us when something was defined, not how good it is.

advanced_nuance: Predefined does not mean permanently unchangeable. A predefined rule can be revised before a later activity begins.
Predefined highlights advance specification. In the source, the absence of predefined labels is relevant; the word does not name the learning method by itself.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a list already written before anyone starts the task.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: We assessed the entries using predefined criteria.
memory_practice.recall_question: Does predefined tell you that something is correct, or that it was specified beforehand?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A team invents the scoring rules only after seeing all the results. Were those rules predefined for that assessment? Explain the timing.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short instruction for a fictional form that uses predefined options. Tell the user what to choose and what to do if no option fits.

examples.example_1: The form asks applicants to choose from a predefined list of categories.
examples.example_2: The judges scored each performance using predefined criteria so that everyone faced the same requirements.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Can I type my own category into this form?
B: No, you must choose one of the predefined options.
A: Then I’ll check the list before I submit it.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We can also use machine learning to find patterns in data without predefined labels.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: decided or established before an activity begins
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker describes finding patterns without labels that were specified beforehand. Without tells us that these predefined labels are absent in the method being described.

mistakes_differences.correction: Say Please choose a predefined option. Predefined is an adjective here and needs the thing being described.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Predefined means defined beforehand. Predicted means expected to happen; deciding a rule in advance is different from predicting a result.

semanticReview.finding: Advance specification distinguished from prediction and correctness; adjective grammar repaired without inventing a source method.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.englishMeaning: used to say that an uncertain action has enough possible benefit to attempt
entry.coreIdea: A small effort with a possible payoff.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Conversational evaluation that an attempt has enough potential benefit to justify trying, despite uncertainty.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Encouraging: it favours attempting the action without promising success.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Tentatively optimistic here: “may still have” identifies a possibility worth checking.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common everyday and workplace English. It is suitable for modest suggestions, not a guarantee about the outcome.

when_to_use: Suggest asking a shop about a spare part without promising availability. A model in this sense: It is worth a try; soaking the jar may loosen the label.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it is worth a try as a promise that the attempt will succeed.
If an attempt carries serious cost or risk, explain why you think its possible benefit justifies trying it.

advanced_nuance: It is worth a try weighs the possible benefit against the effort or cost of attempting something. It can recommend an attempt even when success is unlikely.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A small effort with a possible payoff.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: It is worth a try; soaking the jar may loosen the label.
memory_practice.production_task: Suggest asking a shop about a spare part without promising availability. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: used to say that an uncertain action has enough possible benefit to attempt. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: A shop might have the part you need, and checking takes a short phone call. Which is better supported: It is worth a try, or It is certain to work? Explain the uncertainty.

examples.scenario: It is worth a try; the shop may still have a spare part.
examples.another_setting: It is worth a try; soaking the jar may loosen the label.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: It is worth a try; soaking the jar may loosen the label.
B: I will leave it in warm water for a few minutes.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: It is worth a try; the shop may still have a spare part.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: used to say that an uncertain action has enough possible benefit to attempt
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker suggests contacting the shop because a spare part might still be available. The attempt seems worthwhile even though success is uncertain.

mistakes_differences.correction: It is worth a try, or it is worth trying.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Worth a try judges the attempt worthwhile; likely to work predicts success.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: It is worth a try; it is worth + -ing (It is worth asking)

semanticReview.finding: Valid natural examples, conversation, correction and production retained; uncertainty and cost-benefit judgement clarified.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.englishMeaning: data reserved for tuning and comparing a model during development
entry.coreIdea: Hold data aside to guide model choices during development.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Technical noun phrase for data held aside during development to tune or compare models.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: “validation” names a development role, not proof that the model is correct in every situation.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Instructional here: the speaker distinguishes training, tuning and final testing roles.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Standard machine-learning terminology. Preserve its distinction from the separate test set described in the same sentence.

when_to_use: Name data held aside to compare model choices or guide tuning during development.
when_not_to_use: Do not describe a final test set as a validation set while also claiming it remained untouched during model selection. Keep the roles clear.

advanced_nuance: Repeatedly choosing changes that improve one validation set can make the model too closely suited to that set. A good validation score is not a guarantee of future performance.
Validation set describes the role of the data. Its useful size and composition depend on the task; the term does not prescribe one fixed percentage.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture three labelled groups: learn, choose, then check.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: We compared the two models on the validation set.
memory_practice.recall_question: Which development decision can results from a validation set help you make?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A team uses reserved data to choose between two model settings. Is that data serving as a validation set or an untouched final test set? Explain its role.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short note to a new team member explaining what the validation set will be used for and why the final test set should stay separate.

examples.example_1: We compared two model settings on the validation set before choosing which one to keep.
examples.example_2: The image team reserved a validation set to check whether changes improved recognition during development.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Which of these settings should we use?
B: Let’s compare their results on the validation set.
A: Good. We’ll keep the test set for the final evaluation.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: And once the data is cleaned and structured, it's split into a training set to build a model, a validation set to tune it, and the test set to evaluate final performance.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: data reserved for tuning and comparing a model during development
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker separates three roles: training builds the model, validation guides tuning, and testing checks final performance. The validation set helps the team choose settings during development.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Misleading: We repeatedly chose settings using the validation set, so its score is an independent final test.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say The validation set guided our choices; a separate test set is reserved for the final check. Data used to choose settings is not an untouched final evaluation.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: The training set is used to fit the model. The validation set guides choices during development, while the separate test set estimates final performance in the workflow described here.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: evaluate a model on + a validation set; reserve data for + the validation set

semanticReview.finding: Training, tuning and final-testing roles separated; validation reuse limits explained without prescribing a split percentage.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.englishMeaning: used to express the same idea in a clearer or different way
entry.coreIdea: Same idea in a clearer box.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Discourse marker introducing a restatement: the second sentence explains what conditional funding means in practical terms.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it signals clarification rather than necessarily disagreement.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Clarifying and direct here: the speaker translates the condition into a requirement to meet targets.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and widely usable in conversation and writing. The restatement should preserve the original meaning.

when_to_use: Restate a point using clearer wording or explain its practical meaning without changing the claim.
when_not_to_use: Do not introduce an unrelated extra fact with in other words.
Do not turn may into will or some into all while claiming merely to restate the original idea.

advanced_nuance: In other words signals that the speaker sees two formulations as equivalent. A listener can still challenge the restatement if it makes the original claim stronger or narrower.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Same idea in a clearer box.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The ticket is non-transferable. In other words, only you can use it.
memory_practice.production_task: Tell a colleague that funding will be released only after agreed targets are met. Then use in other words to restate that condition in simpler language.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: used to express the same idea in a clearer or different way. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: The service may be delayed. Which restatement preserves the claim? A: In other words, a delay is possible. B: In other words, it will definitely arrive late. Explain the difference.

examples.scenario: The funding is conditional. In other words, we must meet the agreed targets.
examples.another_setting: The ticket is non-transferable. In other words, only you can use it.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: The ticket is non-transferable. In other words, only you can use it.
B: Understood; I will not give it to my friend.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: The funding is conditional. In other words, we must meet the agreed targets.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: used to express the same idea in a clearer or different way
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker explains the funding condition as a requirement to meet agreed targets. In other words introduces a clearer restatement of what the condition means here.

mistakes_differences.correction: In other words, only you can use it.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: In another words, only you can use it.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: In other words restates meaning; moreover adds a new supporting point.

semanticReview.finding: Valid examples and grammar contrast retained; concrete restatement task rejects unwarranted strengthening of a claim.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.

entry.englishMeaning: a recurring problem that causes difficulty or frustration for users or customers
entry.coreIdea: Picture the repeated snag in a customer's journey.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative business phrase for a recurring source of difficulty or frustration, rather than physical pain.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative toward the problem: it highlights something users want improved.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Problem-focused here: “major” emphasizes how much delayed updates inconvenience customers.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common business and product vocabulary, but jargon to some audiences. “Recurring customer problem” is plainer.

when_to_use: Describe a communication pain point and suggest one way to reduce it.
A natural model: Finding the right form is the main pain point for new members.
when_not_to_use: Do not call a requested feature a pain point without identifying the user problem it would solve.
Use a plainer phrase such as recurring problem if the audience is unfamiliar with product or service terminology.

advanced_nuance: A pain point describes the user’s difficulty, not a particular solution. Several different changes may address the same pain point, so describing the problem clearly helps a team compare options.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture the repeated snag in a customer's journey.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Finding the right form is the main pain point for new members.
memory_practice.production_task: Describe a communication pain point and suggest one way to reduce it. Use the target expression in one or two sentences. Check its pattern and register only after speaking.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking, retrieve the expression meaning a recurring problem that causes difficulty or frustration for users or customers. Then say it in a new situation.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Users repeatedly fail to find the correct form. Is the pain point their difficulty finding it, or the proposed new search button? Explain the difference between a problem and one possible solution.

examples.scenario: Long waits for updates are a major customer pain point.
examples.another_setting: Finding the right form is the main pain point for new members.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Finding the right form is the main pain point for new members.
B: Could we put all the forms on one page?

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Long waits for updates are a major customer pain point.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: a recurring problem that causes difficulty or frustration for users or customers
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Customers repeatedly have to wait too long for updates. The speaker identifies that frustrating part of the service as a problem to improve.

mistakes_differences.correction: We need to address this pain point.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: We need to address to this pain point.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A pain point is experienced friction; a proposed feature is only one possible response.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: pain point: identify/address + a pain point

semanticReview.finding: Valid examples, conversation and address grammar retained; user difficulty distinguished from a proposed feature.
semanticReview.scope: All eight sections and changed headers; no audio or local import verification.
